title: Krishna Is Born at Midnight
story:
At the stroke of midnight a child was born in the prison of Mathura, and outside, where almost no one was watching, the world began to change. The dark lay over the city like a held breath, and then, very quietly, it began to give way.

The sky cleared of its clouds, and the stars came out bright and close. The rivers, stirred and clouded all day, settled until their water ran clear as glass, and the ponds opened their lotus flowers like ornaments laid out for a guest. Far off, the seas took up a low, peaceful murmur, as if they too were singing. A wind rose, gentle and cool to the touch, carrying a clean, sweet scent, so that anyone awake at that hour would have breathed it in and wondered what had changed. Even the hearth fires that had gone cold across the city were said to kindle again with a mild flame, and a soft light spread over the whole earth, as though moonlight had been poured across it. In their homes, good people felt a long and private worry lift from their minds, without knowing why.

Inside the prison, none of this could be seen. The cell was small and dark, and there Devaki lay with her newborn child. She and her husband Vasudeva had been shut away by her brother Kamsa, who ruled Mathura and who lived in terror of a prophecy: that Devaki's eighth child would be his death. One by one he had killed the children she had borne before this one, dashing them as soon as they came into the world, so that no child could grow into the doom that had been promised to him. Each birth in that room had ended the same way, and still the child came.

The night of that birth would be kept ever after as Jayanti, the most blessed night of the year, and those who read the stars named its hour Vijaya, the victorious, with the star Abhijit standing over it. The child came quietly, without trumpets or attendants, as quietly as the full moon rises over the rim of the world. But beyond the cell, the world seemed to know. Unseen above the prison, the musicians of heaven sang, the sages and the gods let showers of flowers drift down from the sky, and somewhere a celestial horn sounded, though no hand had touched it.

None of that singing reached the streets of Mathura. The city slept, and the king slept, and the guards kept their watch at the prison doors, unaware that the hour they had been set to guard against had already come. The only witnesses to that joy were the two prisoners in the cell and the quiet elements of the world.

Yet something had entered the world that the wind, the rivers, and the stars all seemed to recognize, and the night itself had turned gentle to receive it.
reflection: The birth is told almost entirely through what the world did not see: a sky clearing, winds turning gentle, rivers settling. The wonder is not announced to the city but to the elements, and it is all the more moving for being unheard.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds that when Vasudeva first looked upon the child he beheld a four-armed form holding the conch, discus and mace, and begged him to conceal it; that moment is told separately in this collection.
next_story_tease: But the night was not over: the river still lay between the child and safety.
hero_scene: A newborn Krishna in the dark of the prison cell while, unseen beyond the walls, the night turns calm: stars brighten, rivers settle, and flowers drift down from the sky.
visual_elements: flowers falling unseen from the sky
